title: The Danger of Memory and Lust
english: [It] will neigh when moved by a passionate impulse.

Chapter 4. On fornication. Self-control gives birth to temperance, but gluttony is the mother of licentiousness; oil nourishes a lamp’s flame, and the company of women kindles a torch of pleasure. The violence of waves distresses an unballasted ship, and a thought of fornication [distresses] an incontinent mind. Fornication will take satiety as an ally; for it will abandon him and stand with the enemies, and in the end will make war together with the foes. He who loves stillness remains unwounded by the enemy’s arrows, but he who mingles with a crowd receives continual wounds.

The sight of a woman is a poisoned arrow; it has wounded the soul and deposited its venom, and the longer it lingers, the more putrefaction it works. He who guards against these arrows does not visit public festivals, nor does he go about gaping at the feasts; for it is better to remain at home and devote oneself to prayers than, thinking to honor the feasts, to become the enemies’ by-product. Flee the company of women if you wish to be temperate, and do not give them boldness to be bold toward you ever. For at first they either have or pretend reverence; but later they dare all things shamelessly.

At the first meeting they keep their gaze down, speak gently, weep sympathetically, comport themselves reverently, sigh bitterly, ask about chastity, and listen eagerly; the second time you saw [them], and they lifted [their eyes] slightly upward; the third, and they pay attention shamelessly — you smiled, and they laughed unrestrainedly; then they adorn themselves and show themselves to you openly, shaping their gaze to proclaim the passion, raising their eyebrows and rolling their eyelids, baring their necks and preening with their whole bodies, speaking words that soften toward passion and practicing a voice that charms the hearing, until through all these they besiege the soul. These become hooks baiting you toward death, and many-tangled snares drawing you toward destruction. Let them not lead you astray, having used gentle words; for a malignant venom of beasts is hidden in them.

Chapter 5. Approach a burning fire rather than a young woman, being young yourself; for having approached fire and been pained, you will quickly leap away, but having been made soft by womanish words, you will not easily depart. A plant standing by water flourishes, and the passion of licentiousness [flourishes] in the company of women.

He who fills his belly and promises to be temperate is like one who claims to bridle the working of fire in straw. For just as it is impossible to check the rush of fire running in straw, so it is impossible to stop an uncontrolled impulse burning in satiety. A pillar is supported by its base, and the passion of fornication rests upon satiety. A storm-tossed ship hastens to harbor, and the soul of the temperate seeks the desert; the one flees waves of the sea threatening danger, the other forms of women causing painful destruction. An adorned form sinks [one] worse than a wave; for from the wave it is even possible to swim away, out of longing for life, but a woman’s form, having deceived, persuades [one] to despise even life itself. A desert bramble escapes the flame of fire unharmed, and the temperate man separated from women has not been inflamed by the passion of licentiousness; for just as the memory of fire does not burn the mind, so a passion has no strength when its fuel is absent.

Chapter 6. If you pity an enemy, he will become your foe, and if you spare a passion, it will rise up against you. The sight of a woman provokes the licentious toward pleasure, but the temperate — even there — toward the glorification of God; if the passion grows calm in the company of women, do not trust it when it promises dispassion. For even a dog wags [its tail] when left with a crowd, but having come outside, it displays its own wickedness. When the memory of a woman comes to you without passion, then consider that you have reached the bounds of temperance. But when her image rouses you to contemplation, and her arrows encompass your soul, then consider that you are outside virtue. But do not even so linger over such thoughts, nor converse long in your mind with a woman’s form; for the passion is fond of turning back, and has danger near. For just as measured smelting purifies silver, but prolonged [smelting] easily destroys it, so a lingering fantasy of a woman corrupts a temperate habit; nor converse long with the face that appeared, lest it kindle in you a flame of pleasure and set fire to the threshing-floor of your soul; for just as a spark lingering in chaff raises a flame, so a remaining memory of a woman kindles desire.
Chapter 7. On love of money. Love of money is the root of all evils (1 Tim 6:10), and it nourishes the remaining passions as evil branches, and will not let what has blossomed from it wither.

title: The Monk of Silver-Loving and the Nature of Anger
english: He who wishes to cut down the passions, let him cut out the root; for while love of money remains, pruning the branches profits nothing — even if they are cut, they will immediately blossom again. A rich monk is a laden ship, easily sinking in a squall of waves; for just as an overloaded ship is tormented by every wave, so the rich man is submerged by anxieties. An ungreedy monk is a well-equipped traveler, finding lodging in every place. An ungreedy monk is a high-flying eagle, swooping down for food only when need compels.

Such a one is higher than every temptation; he laughs at present things, is lifted up on high, departs from earthly things, and roams together with those above; for he has a light wing, not weighed down by anxieties; tribulation came, and he left the place without grief; death stood by, and he departs cheerfully; for he bound his soul to no earthly bond.

But the rich man is fettered by anxieties, and is tied like a dog to a chain; even if he is forced to move away, he carries the memories of his possessions as a heavy burden and a useless load; he is stung by grief and pained violently at the thought; he has left his possessions and is scourged by grief. And if death comes, he piteously leaves present things, gives up his soul, and does not turn his eye from his affairs; unwilling, he is dragged like a runaway slave; he is separated from his body but not separated from his affairs — the more so as the passion holds back those who drag him.

Chapter 8. The sea is not filled, receiving a multitude of rivers, and the desire of the money-lover is not filled with money; he has doubled his money and desires to make it double again, and never ceases doubling, until death stops this fruitless haste.

A sensible monk will attend to the need of the body, and fill the want of the stomach with bread and water; he will not flatter the rich for the pleasure of the belly, nor enslave a free mind to many masters; for the hands suffice to serve the body and to fill its natural need continually. An ungreedy monk is an unhindered athlete and a light runner, swiftly reaching the prize of the upward calling. A rich monk rejoices in many revenues, but the ungreedy in crowns of achievements.

A money-loving monk works hard, but the ungreedy devotes himself to prayers and readings. A money-loving monk fills chests with gold, but the ungreedy stores treasure in heaven. ‘Accursed is he who makes an idol and sets it in secret’ (Deut 27:15), and likewise he who has the passion of love of money; for the one worships a counterfeit, useless thing, while the other carries about an image of the fantasy of wealth.

Chapter 9. On anger. Anger is a maddening passion, and easily drives out of their senses those who have knowledge; it makes the soul bestial and makes [one] avoid every encounter. A violent wind will not move a tower, and thumos does not snatch away a wrathless soul. Water is moved by the violence of winds, and the irascible man is troubled by senseless thoughts. An angry monk saw someone and gnashed his teeth. The rising of mist thickens the air, and the movement of thumos [thickens] the mind of the angry man. A cloud slipping beneath darkened the sun, and a thought of rancor [darkened] the mind. A lion in a cage stirs continually, and the irascible man in his cell stirs thoughts of anger. A pleasant sight is a calm sea, but nothing is more pleasant than a peaceful state; for in a calm sea dolphins swim about, and in a peaceful state god-befitting thoughts swim. A long-suffering monk is a quiet spring, offering all a gentle drink; but the mind of the angry man is continually troubled and will not give water to the thirsty — and if it gives, it is muddied and useless; and the eyes of the irascible are troubled and bloodshot, messengers of the troubled heart. But the face of the long-suffering is rightly composed, and his eyes are gentle, looking downward.

Chapter 10. A man’s gentleness is remembered by God, and a wrathless soul becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit. Christ lays His head to rest in a long-suffering spirit, and a peacemaking mind becomes a dwelling of the Holy Trinity. Foxes dwell in a rancorous soul, and beasts make their lair in a troubled heart. A reverent man flees a shameful lodging, and God [flees] a rancorous heart. A stone falling in troubled water, and an evil word [troubled] a man’s heart. Remove thoughts of anger from your soul, and let thumos not encamp in your heart, and you will not be troubled in the time of prayer; for just as the smoke of chaff troubles the eyes, so…

title: The Dangers of Passion and the Nature of Acedia
english: …does rancor [trouble] the mind in the time of prayer. The thoughts of the irascible are the offspring of a viper, and they devour the heart that bore them. The prayer of the irascible is an abominable incense; and the psalmody of the angry is a graceless sound. The gift of the rancorous is a sacrifice swarming [with ants], and it shall not approach altars sprinkled around. The irascible sees troubled dreams, and the angry imagines the onsets of beasts. A long-suffering man sees visions — encounters with holy angels — and the rancorless trains himself in spiritual words, and in the night receives the solutions of mysteries.

Chapter 11. On sadness. A grieving monk knows not spiritual pleasure; sadness is the dejection of the soul, and it is composed of thoughts of anger; for thumos is the appetite for revenge, and the failure of revenge gave birth to sadness; sadness is a lion’s mouth, and easily swallows the grieving one. Sadness is a worm of the heart, and devours the mother that bore it. A mother giving birth to a child is in pain; once she has given birth, she is released from the pain; but sadness, once born, stirs up much pain, and remaining after the birth-pangs, it pains not a little. A grieving monk knows not spiritual joy, just as one burning with fever [knows not] the taste of honey. A grieving monk will not move his mind toward contemplation, nor send up a pure prayer; for sadness is a hindrance to every good. A fetter on the feet is a hindrance to running, and sadness a hindrance to contemplation. A captive of barbarians is bound with irons, and a captive of the passions is bound with sadness. Sadness has no strength when the other passions are absent, just as a bond has none when those who bind are absent. He who is bound by sadness has been conquered by the passions, and carries his bond as the proof of his defeat. For sadness is composed upon the failure of fleshly appetite; and appetite is yoked to every passion. He who has conquered appetite has conquered the passions, and he who has conquered the passions will not be mastered by sadness. The self-controlled does not grieve at the failure of foods, nor the temperate when he misses licentious folly, nor the wrathless when he falls short of revenge, nor the humble when deprived of human honor, nor the ungreedy when he meets with loss — for they have strongly turned aside from the appetite for these things; for just as one wearing a breastplate does not receive an arrow, so the dispassionate is not wounded by sadness.
Chapter 12. A shield is safety for a soldier, and a wall for a city; but dispassion is safer for a monk than both;

for an arrow rushing with a whir has often pierced a shield, and a multitude of warriors has demolished a wall, but sadness will not prevail against dispassion. He who masters the passions has mastered sadness, but he who is defeated by pleasure will not escape its bonds. He who grieves continually and pretends dispassion is like one who is sick and feigns health; for just as the sick man is revealed by his complexion, so the passionate is exposed by sadness. He who loves the world will grieve much, but he who despises what is in it will rejoice continually. The money-lover who has suffered loss will grieve bitterly, but he who despises money will be without grief. The glory-lover will grieve when dishonor comes, but the humble will receive it as a companion. A smelting-pot purified base silver, and godly sadness [purifies] a heart in sins; continual smelting diminishes lead, and worldly sadness diminishes the mind. Darkness dims the working of the eyes, and sadness dulls the contemplative mind; the sun’s light does not pierce the depth of water, and the contemplation of light does not illumine a grief-stricken heart; sweet to all men is the sunrise, but even at this a grieving soul is displeased. Jaundice takes away the sense of taste, and sadness takes away the soul’s perception. But he who despises the pleasures of the world will not be troubled by thoughts of sadness.

Chapter 13. On acedia. Acedia is the weakness of the soul; and the weakness of a soul that does not have what is according to nature does not stand nobly against temptations. For what food is to a healthy body, that temptation is to a noble soul. The north wind nourishes crops, and temptations confirm the endurance of the soul. A waterless cloud is driven by the wind, and a mind without endurance [is driven] by the spirit of acedia. Spring dew increases the fruit of the field, and a spiritual word exalts the state of the soul. A current of acedia drives the monk out of his house, but he who has endurance rests continually. The acedia-stricken puts forward visits to the sick, but fulfills his own purpose. An acedia-stricken monk is keen for service, and counts his own satisfaction as a commandment; a slight breeze bent a weak plant, and a fantasy of going abroad drew the acedia-stricken. A well-rooted tree was not shaken by the violence of winds, and…
